sp.p: That makes no difference. I mystify the old man, then he tells me the name without knowing it. That is a not yet completely worn-out artifice, of which I therefore need not be ashamed.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Madman!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Double-tongue!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, I am still not so now, not for you, not for your request, which is sufficiently known to me. You want to marry my niece, and with her, her not inconsiderable fortune.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Will not let himself be made known. The direction of the plan is my work alone. You are the person following me.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: One moment! The letter that was mentioned before might perhaps give us light; if only we had it!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But won't you tell me beforehand – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Your word in honor, if it were true; but it is only half true. I want only your niece and ask – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Glorious idea! Away, to see if I can steal it away from the old man.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Oh, please don't take it amiss! I just thought we were standing on the stage, and there it's not uncommon in a situation like ours for things to go thus between master and servant.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: As you please.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Indeed I am that; yet one must not totally violate the sense of duty.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: It is useless effort; for I will be relentless, even if you stand on your head.

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.stage: (takes his master's hat and stick, which he had placed on the table, wipes over the hat with his sleeve, hands both to him and asks:)
sp.p: Do you command anything else?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: „To serve!“ Through this word alone can a cunning servant justify his loose mouth against his master. „To serve!“ he says and thereby commits some action that proves his distance from his master.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What, my lord? You have the audacity to come here? even to ask for me?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Why exactly that?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What have you to find fault with in me?

Successfully snatched! A chambermaid who knows only half her old household master's weaknesses must be able to make such innocent thievish moves blindly. – Where then is my comedy player? Already gone? – – Oh dear! I hear a commotion. It's the old man. Away through the back door before he notices me with the letter. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I entreat you, yield to my petition. I am well able to maintain my future wife –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: You are insufferable to me!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But I shall take flight with her as soon as she is free.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Not nearly as much as I would have to be to resemble your comedy guardians.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That I shall keep to myself.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That I shall do; but never at your command.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: You are very short with me.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I am just that way, and to put an end to this conversation, learn that your Dulcinea remains imprisoned until – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The bridegroom.

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.stage: (who shows himself in his true form)
sp.p: Your most obedient servant's clever work.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What do you want here then?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What? You here? Now?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: You are a cruel man, an unchristian, a Turk, a tyrant!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I withdraw –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Why does the bridegroom hesitate to enter? Should I perhaps go to meet him?

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.stage: (fantastically attired; the more striking, the better, even should his costume be ever so improbable, yes, even absurd: such things find favour. The shaping of outward forms leads to the highest degree of art.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Welcome, welcome! You are – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The young gentleman approaches –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Closer! closer!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, I do not comprehend you. Do I not wholly enter into the spirit of the present world of fashions, of novels, and of comedies? Do I not do all that an uncle and guardian must do, in order to be interesting?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: – but I return.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The bridegroom enters the house.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Bring him in to me.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Though I am delighted by your punctual arrival, I am yet somewhat astonished at – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The suitor is already entering the house.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: This way! Into this room! Open!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Let yourself be entreated. My lawsuit may not yet be won, but I am nonetheless able to provide for my future wife. – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That I would be a fool to answer such a question.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Indeed! in order to enlighten you about yourself. Can it have been reasonable of you to ask again for a name which you must already know? A needless questioner, sir, is the most insipid pedant – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Beyond doubt you know my name. A letter from my father has been in your hands since yesterday, or the day before –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well yes, of course, but – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Fiekchen, off with you! To such a question no man responds, who, like me, has seen the world both from the front and from the rear.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: And were you steeped in gold to your very ears. I have firmness of character, and am therefore no comedy-uncle, and I will not give you the girl.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You still doubt that my name is known to you? As though my father had not written to you but lately!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed; however – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense without end! But did you wish to hear this question from my own lips?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You see! And yet you would again have had to ask me what my name is.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: As though another might not present himself in my stead, to deceive you, to betray me, to delude us both –?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Sir, your laconic manner shall have an end. Necessity will compel you to open the prison of my beloved.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Not in the slightest.

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.p: But let all quarrel be put aside. I am to have the honour of becoming related to you. I might again instructively remark that your young niece is necessary for that, and that you have not yet even introduced me to her. But surely you intend now to lead me to her.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, you are driving me mad.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: At your service, sir. My niece shall be here directly. Call her forth! (He whispers into the chambermaid’s ear and secretly hands her a key)

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I shall be back this instant. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Oh yes, I shall. But not a second sooner than I see fit.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: A man like me consults only with himself. But you, you must listen to me.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: No, I say; for my niece shall follow me, shall give you her hand, and the notary shall at once – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What? You do not deem it worth the trouble to love me? Me, of all men? Do you know who I am? I am the young Lord of **, the best, most excellent, most learned, most well-read, most experienced, most amiable, most incomparable, most inimitable, most perfect son of my father; for I am his only son, and therefore – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Just calmly now, sir. My niece shall reconsider, let her but find words.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Your assured bridegroom, famed through all parts of the world; for I have been in every part of it, and cannot brook the delay of becoming yours. So give me your hand, and – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: There’s no managing that man.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: And yet you wish to marry me to him?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: All is prepared for my flight with her. The moment she is free, I drive with her to the border and have myself joined to her in wedlock.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What contract? What notary? My hand is given by love alone, not by a sheet of paper, even if every authority in the world had stamped it.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: We shall see about that, young sir. You are short of speech; I will be shorter still. You will not have my niece? That remains to be seen. You will hardly, I trust, rebel against your father? And he desires this marriage, therefore you must submit.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Quite right. Bridegroom and bride. Make haste, that they be made husband and wife.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Let the gentleman speak on as he will. He has heard my no, and I have nothing further to say to him.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Rebellious fool!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, allow yourself to be advised –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I do not wish to, do not want it, will not do it!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Mad scheme, in which there is nothing clever, except that you betrayed it to me in advance. Yet you shall learn that quite another shall lead my niece home as bride, that he is the one contracted, and that he is coming.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Out of my sight.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That I shall not do. I shall come at you. You have contracted me, and I remain, since I am here. The prescription for your final hour you dictated to my pen yourself; as a skilled apothecary, I shall mix you the draught by which you shall be transformed into a corpse –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You own a stable, I know it, a splendid one: Very well! On my wedding day I shall nail shut every one of your horses, and shall leave you no substitute save the lamest mare I can find within ten miles around.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Madman!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: And should I not succeed, then I shall smear butter upon the horses' hay –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, I shall throw you out of the house.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That is something else entirely. That I shall accept, for then I need not marry the damsel. So go ahead; throw me out!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Be not uneasy! You have not yet come to your last shirt; but I shall know how to make you long for it. Every joy of your life will I salt, pepper, spoil, and embitter! I know you are no friend to wind instruments, you fall into convulsions when you hear them: Well then! I will sound the hunting-horn – Trurutrutru! I shall find ways to unnerve you.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Your register has a hole! says Spiegelberg or Glasberg. You’ve left out the bridegroom. What if he now arrives?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You and I, truthfully, shall not remain here.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Most certainly not!

div.head: Final Scene.
div.stage: The Lover. The Niece. The Chambermaid. The Servant.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: How came it all so suddenly?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: No matter! he will not overtake us: we shall be far gone by then –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Far away, to the sanctuary of love!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He is here already.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Heaven’s messenger! Take this eight-groschen piece for such tidings. It is really he, is it not?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed! In One Act, and titled?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Without further ado: The Lover and his Servant.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Too much honour for me.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well then: Lackey’s Wit and Chambermaid’s Cunning.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I beg you to leave me out of this game. I did nothing in it, save pilfer a letter which we did not even need.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: And what I did in all this was chiefly done to win your hand, dearest little rogue. So let the play be called All for His Girl, after the Spanish: Todo por su dama. That will sound strange to the audience. But so much the likelier shall they applaud.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Of course it is I, my lady.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dearest confidante, shall I ever possess him?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Oh certainly; the bridegroom –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: My uncle’s intention – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Here I am. Without me, it will not do.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Fortune demands time. –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Did you hear the message from that saucy mouth? What now, young sir?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Yes, if only my stern uncle would not –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Ah! in your way, I see no way out.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Let me embrace you!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Beloved of my heart!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: But heavens, why are you here?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Those cursed letters of my uncle!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dearest, do you still care for me?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Excess is harmful, even in love. – Let us rather put it to the test now – –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: By no means. I will be wiser than many another love-sick girl. I will not rashly throw my rich dowry to the winds. So let us think upon some means.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Out of caution, lest the old man suspect anything, who caught me with my servant upon the stairs.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What is your command, dear Uncle?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: The son of his friend must absolutely receive my hand: thus wills my uncle.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Hush! I am no foolish lover from Friedrich Jünger’s "Abduction". I have a purpose, and purpose must have its due, so I, my marriage portion. Therefore we must devise a plan.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Let us flee; seek a sanctuary where love may dwell untroubled – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: But where, then, is the young gentleman?

sp.speaker: The Uncle
sp.stage: (entering with an open letter in his hand)
sp.p: That is true: My old friend von Eschen moves slowly, yet surely. How he writes here, how he has decked out his son before sending him forth to woo! Welcome then, young Mr. Jeremias! To arrive to-morrow, perhaps even to-day? Well and good! I would you were already here, that my ward’s coquetries might have an end; for she must take you, Mr. Jeremias. You are worthy, wealthy, well brought up, fairly brimming with knowledge of every kind – what an excellent match for my niece. – But where is she? She is wont to be here at this hour? – Hallo! (He rings. The Cchambermaid appears in the doorway.) I would speak with my niece, at once!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: As you command. (Exit)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I will make her plainly and roundly understand my ultimatum in this matter.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dearest Uncle – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well then, take her, but get that fellow there (pointing to the Servant) out of my sight.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: With pleasure.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: And you too, no doubt, shall soon depart with your cara amata? –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: My life’s happiness – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Schnetterdeng! sounded the postilion’s horn. The passengers dismounted, a young gentleman asked the coachman a brief question; he pointed with his finger, and the young gentleman now makes his way toward our house.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Larifari!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Tears, indeed, Mademoiselle?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: His case is decided, be it in his favour or to his detriment; for in either event – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Lies in the hands of your betrothed, who with each passing second draws nearer –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I pity you. You went out for wool and return home shorn. But why did you go for wool at all, when there were no sheep for you to shear?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Be calm. When the bridal gown is finished, the hour of your resurrection shall also strike.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Say rather an unhappy, a singularly unhappy –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: You are consigning me to death.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Only a postponement, dearest Uncle.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I take my leave –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense! „Maiden, do you take the present gentleman, Mr. **, to be your wedded husband?“ – The dead awoke! Answer: Yes!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: By no means! A preposterous one.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: If my good mother could see how you treat me!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – to become wretched –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Adieu!

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Away, Mademoiselle, you shall be dealt with accordingly.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – That must yield to your tyrannical decree of power –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dear Uncle, I implore you! is this a just proceeding?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But I shall return.

Only a moment. He is gone. I shall call at once, if indeed the air is entirely clear. (at the cabinet) Yes, the old man has gone upstairs. It is his hour for reading the newspaper. – Quick now! Come closer! Is your master with you?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Then take her, so I may have peace from the madman. – Adieu, Sir. You too shall soon depart, dear children?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Most gracious Princess Contradiction, the comedy draws to its end; make haste, lest you be hissed from the stage. Be sensible!

div.head: Ninth Scene.
div.stage: The Chambermaid. The Lover. The Servant.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That will not be necessary.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Alas! her lovely freedom is gone.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Be calm! Where there is love, there is also stratagem; and at times embarrassment: Kotzebue knew that well enough, why should not we?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: There are master and servant!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Help, and rely upon your master's generosity. If I even do you an additional service, he will surely not fail to reward you handsomely.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The young gentleman enters the house.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Bring him up!!

div.head: Ninth Scene.
div.stage: The Chambermaid. The Lover. The Servant.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Quickly, let me hear –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Not as with young squire Hans von Birken do I mean to act out a sentimental play for the suitor. Nothing of the sort! I know a better course.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: My ear listened, my heart pounded, out of vexation, mind you. Do not imagine it pounded from anything else. Our young lady’s betrothed approaches, tomorrow – perhaps even today.

sp.speaker: The Servant
sp.stage: (in a ridiculous attire, pieced together from every fashion journal of Europe, quite in the manner of our beardless aesthetes and fine spirits, who, as is well known, despise the laws of unity in the realm of true beauty as the idle fancies of some obsolete Greek classic, since a true aesthete, as everyone knows, need not understand Greek at all.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: How happy I am to finally be able to welcome you.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: So think I as well. I will wage a noble battle for my master and lord.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Yes, yes, let us know – – The walls here have no ears, do they?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: How shall we deter the young squire from dipping into the dish set before him?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Yes. Here he stands. It is I, I play the fine gentleman, Mr. ** – – what is his name?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: My lord, I come to bring you joy. Observe me. Attend me. Hear me. How do I please you?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Witling!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Scoundrel!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: For heaven’s sake! have mercy on me!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Never, not unless you relent. You will not spare yourself, how, then, can I spare you?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Who cared about the name!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Braggart!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Buffoon!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, a little astonishment, which you inspire in me, aside, I am delighted – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: So it was you?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: A fine idea!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: All the same! Such fellows are usually called von Birken, or Bocklümmel, or Feldkümmel –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Do it; but it must be done quickly. Once you have him, toss him to me over the garden wall.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Astonishment? Rapture? What is the meaning of this? How says the Frenchman? What must you become upon beholding me? troublé, cajolé, écrasé, mortifié, massacré, transformé, analysé – sacré nom de Dieu! How says the Englishman? troubled, bubbled, coaxed, boxed, plucked, sucked, huddled, puddled, washed, plashed – Bless my soul! – Good morning, Sir – As you like it – All in the wrong – Measure for measure! (pounds the table.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, let us speak sensible German.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That cannot be discussed. You have nothing to do here but to follow me.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: A thought strikes me. What if we could get hold of the letter which my beloved’s uncle received yesterday?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Ah, you dearest of sirs! (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But how so? What have I to do with the affair?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Only patience, sir! No one speaks here now but I. Do you know, sir, that I have come to know the world as well as my toothpick case? The most famous statesmen, for instance, the editor of the "Old "or the "New Firebrands", and the most celebrated writers, for instance, the editor of the "Berlin Express Post", are on familiar terms with me. When those renowned doctors and men of the Order of Merit – pour le mérite – travelled to Brazil, I furnished them with essays on the geography and ethnography of that ancient empire. And where, sir, did I sit when I wrote those essays? Upon my father’s estate at Zippelsdorf in Farther Pomerania, in the cowshed, because at the time I was obliged to undergo a milk cure –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, enough is enough! I wish you were still sitting there.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: To be sure, the title of "Sir" belongs properly to me here; yet I shall be modest.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Fool! and yet not one of the worst sort. Lead the way now!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Is it not a convention in comedies that the servant must have a saucy tongue toward his master? Still, I meant no real offense with you. Forgive me!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Does it please you? Yes!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What objections! What interruptions! Know, Sir, that I am here – at least for this moment – to play the leading part. Had I not come, I would not be here; were I not here, I could not marry your young niece; if I do not marry your young niece, she will, in all likelihood, become an old maid; if she becomes an old maid, she will assuredly grow absurd, foolish, bigoted, slanderous, covetous, envious, miserly, quarrelsome! Who, then, is the main person here? Why, then, do you interrupt me?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: An honour I must first earn. Therefore, I shall not yet make true use of it.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That is the privilege of a cunning servant in comedies, to be a know-it-all. And though we are not actually playing a comedy here, it certainly looks very much as though we were.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I am not so yet. At least not for you. I know what you seek. My ward, and with her no insignificant fortune.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I truly do not know – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nor am I that yet; at least not for you. I know, without a word from your lips, what you want. You want money, and along with it to marry a girl, my ward.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: And were you to beg on bended knee; to kneel and beg till your knees were raw – I say No! No! No!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Foolishness! It will take quite different men than you and I to burst open this prison. Do you know the young Mr. von **? He will be coming.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What do you say?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Why yes indeed, sir! I must speak with you. I inquired after you once already today. I found you not to be seen –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Sad enough! Had you, like myself, a clear faculty of apprehension and a secure talent for exposition, you would deal differently with me. Before all else you would long since have asked me: Sir, who are you? What is your honoured name?

“To steal, one must know the ways, that makes half the work!” is a passage from the Mirror of Virtue for chambermaids, drawn from many one-act farces of famous authors. Whether I’ve understood the passage? I should think so, for the letter is in my hands. The old man laid it beside his pipe. – But where are master and servant? Already gone? Then I must after them. Quick, down the backstairs! (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well then, as soon as she is free, I shall run off with her.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I cannot abide you.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Give heed to me. I am making you the most reasonable representations. True, I am not wealthy, yet I am perfectly able to make a wife happy in every respect.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Heavens above! My bile is rising. So, state your name.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Very categorical!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: You think so? So do I. Then we are of one mind, and you will be glad to learn that your tender shepherdess is under house arrest.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I shall indeed; but not because you desire it. Quite other motives will lead me to it.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He is here!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: In the Swindlers’ Alley a country coach drew up. A young gentleman alighted. He whispered but two words into the ear of the innkeeper at the Unicorn, who thereupon pointed with his finger toward our house, toward which the young gentleman now hastened with quick steps.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That I should be a fool, and give answer to such a question!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Oh, assuredly it is your betrothed!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, it is now time you sought your fortune elsewhere.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He has already arrived.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Truly? What say you?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Why then do you come here once more?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That is enough to drive one mad! Why then would you have me pose this, this very question to you?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I regard you with joyful rapture and with astonishment.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Yet I shall return again.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Your happiness, your lasting happiness, enters your house with me. – How do I appear to you?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What is this? Do you intend to ignore me, misjudge me, laugh at me, mock me, deride me, despise me, put me aside, look down on me –?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Just so. All wish to know everything, no one wishes to know himself. Were you to know yourself properly, you would not make your memory into a lumber-room, into which you fling your notions head over heels, so that in the decisive moment you can never find the right one. True, in that you bear some resemblance to certain German philosophers; but in my presence you ought to be ashamed of it. Your memory should, in all fairness, have told you my name before ever you asked for it.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.stage: (The latter in a ridiculous attire dictated by the newest laws of fashion, such as may be observed on merchant’s apprentices or lads of other trades, on budding young aesthetes from the lower forms, or on certain young gentlemen to whom an inheritance of eighty to a hundred thousand thalers had been guaranteed already in the cradle.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Enter, you blessed one, into my house!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But, when I return –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Quite right; for you have not even inquired after me. Why do you not ask what my name is?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Quite right, merely to prove to you, tout bonnement, how greatly you stand in need of my company, my instruction, my guidance, my assistance, my support; for if you needed none of this, then you would not have asked, since you might have known the answer to your question beforehand.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, how so? How can I know your name?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: In truth, I cannot say.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well then! And you take me for so simple-minded that I should not know whether my father, in so important a matter, mentioned my name in such a letter or not? You would ignore that? Sir, you must make amends for it this instant and tell me what my name is.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: How could it be otherwise? You would gladly take me for confused, and yet you seem to be so a little yourself; otherwise you would, before all else, have asked for my name.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Ergo! – which in plain German means: Irk you! Must not so important a letter contain my significant name? Well then? And therefore, that you may not mislead me, nor any other, nor deceive us both, it is for me to ask. So then, sir, what is my name?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Indeed. Did you not yesterday, or if the post allowed it, already the day before yesterday, receive a letter from my father?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Why yes!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Quite naturally! Can not an impostor, a lover in disguise, pass himself off as me and deceive you?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Quite right! The little maid there would persuade me; but I understand her before she speaks. She would tell me it is time to greet my bride. – Old sir, be quick now, and lead me to her.

div.head: Fifteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Servant. The Niece. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Here the bride – here the bridegroom –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: He must not learn that I shut her in. (aloud) At once, sir. (He secretly slips the chambermaid a key and gives her a sign.)

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: At your command, gracious sir. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Thus then! Can so important a letter possibly omit my name? Never, sir! But why do you withhold it from me? Why do you act as though you did not know it? That is an affront. What would many a man, many an author be without a name? A man’s name is his true property, therefore no one is to be blamed if he deals loosely with his good name; for a man may do with his name what he pleases. But why do you lay hands on my property? Quickly now, return it to me, and tell me what my name is.

div.head: Fifteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Servant. The Niece. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Do you desire to make acquaintance, as is fitting for future spouses?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: How? What do you say?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He goes too far! Truly, he ventures too much. (softly to the servant) Caution!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Never!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What? You still refuse?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: To say no requires no great deliberation; and I have said no, I shall say no – forever!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Foolish girl that you are!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, what are you prattling about? Why, my whole household knows well enough that you are the young Mr. von **!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What is this? You would force me? You would force the young lady? You would force us both? My father is to come to your aid in this? Good! To oppose a father is impossible for me. I shall marry the young lady.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Aha!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What? Surely he will not? Is he possessed?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: But my wedding-day shall be your dying-day! I know it well, you are a lover of the chase. I might waylay you, like Hugo Owl did Carlos in The Guilt – "a flash from the tower" – and you would be gone. Afterwards I might feign that I had slain myself, and the matter would be set aside as antiquated; but no! I have sounder and simpler means to vex you to death. I might, for instance, twist the neck of your favourite hound, Waldmann – the innkeeper where I lodged described him to me exactly – gone you would be, you would die of bile fever; or shorter still, I could ram your rifle with a stump of tallow-candle, so that upon firing you get a blowback that sends you to the sickbed and soon thereafter into the grave.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Mademoiselle, do I hear aright? You would play a romance with me? and a tasteless one at that, in which the true lover is to be the deceived one? Am I not your true lover? Has not your uncle appointed me? Me? a specimen of a perfect youth, such as does not let itself be appointed every day, like the prescription of certain physicians, which is in truth but a directive to the gravedigger, payable à vista?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Now, now! You are bursting in like a door flung off its hinges. When my niece has composed herself and found her words, then – –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Raise no hopes. Even at the altar I shall say no.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Do not listen to the prattle of that silly novel-struck girl!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Is the witch tormenting you?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: By no means, but you shall be made to believe you are bewitched, so hard will I deal with you. I will make an epigram upon you and have it printed, a sharp one, in the Morning, Noon, Evening, and Midnight Journal; further, I will set it to music myself, have it sung in the streets with a barrel-organ, and on the title-page of the pamphlet, which I shall distribute by the thousand for free, I will have your well-hit portrait engraved in tin or copper.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Do you see your error now? Or rather, do you see that your error was in truth no error? that you should have asked after all?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Madman!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or no! I will not have it said of me, as in the tragedy: Your very breath is murder! But I will vex you to death before you celebrate your birthday again.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What? that fellow is a downright fop! And I hear you mean to give your ward to him for a wife? Is it possible? But listen to me! I submit to everything that can be submitted to. I know it – the guardianship accounts (softly) are troubling you. Here is my hand, I will give you a written bond that I have already received your niece’s fortune to the last farthing. Well? Will you at last consent to my marriage with her?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – My wish for –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Take the girl then, upon this condition. But you, young whirlwind – out with you! at once! And as for you two? When do you travel?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The fellow is mad, stark mad. Why then not you, but I; why I and not she?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Who has the right to ask questions here? Only I, sir. I am the spurned one, the mocked one, the derided one, the teased, the tricked, the hounded, the wronged, the torn, the cramped, the oppressed –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What? Sir, you dare speak thus to my face? (to the Uncle) Do you not see that the man has lost his senses? Come to your reason! Abandon this accursed marriage scheme! Give me your ward’s hand and – (softly) for half the dowry I will make out a deed of gift to you.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Heavens above, I hear a stranger has slipped into the house. Perhaps a second Sand – Where is he? (to uncle and niece) You are not wounded, are you? – Who is the gentleman here?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Patience, only patience, you tyrannical old guardian! I shall wage war upon you, since you have declared war upon me. All your favourite pursuits will I attack: your gardening, your library, your picture-collection, your pipe-bowls, and that in unheard-of ingenious ways; even your hunting-hound, Melusine, shall have no peace from me.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Indeed! Suppose now I were a masked lover of your niece, who might wish to snatch her from the bridegroom, and for that end had slipped in here under a borrowed name? Well then, sir? Ought you not in that case to have been cautious – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Stop! Say no more. I fear I have played our game with a poor hand. What then, if the true bridegroom should appear tomorrow?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You have me to thank for this.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: By thunder! What are you saying?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Upon my soul! He goes too far; if only the old man does not notice. (She gives the servant a secret sign.)

div.head: Final Scene.
div.stage: The Lover. The Niece. The Servant. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Do tell me. What brought about this sudden change?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You forget the true bridegroom. And if he should come? Consider, we are not playing a comedy here; we are in the real world.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Hope for everything!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Strict he is, that is true, and his intentions are most unfavourable to you. Besides, late last night he received yet another letter –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Hm! hm! Not another word of our quarrel. Present me to your niece, and you will see that I am no disguised lover of hers.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He will be here shortly.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Indeed, and I arrive at precisely the right moment.

div.titlePart: A Clever Servant Sets His Master Right.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: By all the skies! and she is locked in! You! (He signals to the Chambermaid) – My niece shall appear at once, sir! (secretly into the chambermaid’s ear) Unlock the green room. Here is the key. (aloud) Go, child, bring my niece to us.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: At once, gracious sir. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Alas, there is little pleasant to be hoped for from that quarter;especially if the letter which the postman brought late last night – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Let us leave that aside for now. Your adored one is coming.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Our common interest –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Burning love, which since yesterday afternoon, when you last spoke, has risen to such a height by today! (to herself)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Your niece has surely not already bestowed her heart elsewhere?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Let us not torment ourselves before the time; your lover’s arms are beckoning you.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Joy of love, how you beatify!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Let this embrace speak for me!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: The god of love will stand by us. Press your beloved to your heart.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I shall strike the suitor dead.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: By no means. (entering from the side) He must not learn the truth.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Should I, like a foolish maiden, drain the oil from my household lamp, the very oil with which I might supply it, while I am striving to win my uncle over to my side?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I cannot see how you can hesitate even for a moment to fall in with my plan.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What a mad notion!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.stage: (enters with an open letter in his hand.)
sp.p: Welcome letter, that commands me at last to set the crown upon my work. The bridegroom is coming, today, tomorrow – well then! Now must I, now will I keep the word I gave to my honest sword-hilt, my good old friend Plumper. His son Hans, or Michel, or Lebrecht, or whatever else he may be called, shall have my ward, and the little girl shall not mutter a word. – Hallo! Niece! Where is she hiding? (He rings. The chambermaid enters) My ward, the young lady! Hither at once, without delay!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: At your service. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I am weary of this sentimental trifling. – Well then, my dear niece?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Let the little I can call my own go as it will. With you, I am happy in every condition of life.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Self-will in womankind is detestable to me; yet the coercion of guardians is still more hateful. "Man is born free, is free; may marry whom he pleases!" says a famous poet, whom I intend to publish in an improved edition at Gotha or Stuttgart, where improved translations of renowned foreign classics appear. – Ah, surely your young Miss Niece!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Can you jest while my heart is bleeding?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Does not concern me.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Who with good reason must be called a simpleton, a nowhere-man and a beyond-all-bounds.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Will be your bridegroom’s concern.

div.head: Fifteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Servant. The Niece. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Get to know one another, and at once, that my blessing may lead you to the bridal chamber.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: O, heavens above! Guardian, sir!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Novel nonsense!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Did I hear aright? O, misfortune without equal! – Dearest uncle!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: None of that! Not a day, not an hour!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: At your service, my young lady, I am here to marry you.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: You think I am – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: By no means! No delay! Decided – concluded!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: You bring it about that my last hour is striking.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – a pitiable one, torn to pieces at heart.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: By no means, sir.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What? (softly to her) Don’t you dare!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: You are opening the grave of my youthful bloom.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – to be happy –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – to become a housewife, if she has the skill for it.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Alas, unhappy wretch that I am! What must I hear? You disdain me? I kneel, as it were, before you like Count Leicester before Queen Elizabeth; I stand, as it were, humble and yet high-nosed before you like Essex before that same queen; I am better disposed toward you than Hamlet toward Ophelia, for I do not say to you: "Go to a nunnery." Were it night and were we in a garden, I should be tender toward you like Romeo toward Juliet, but in broad daylight and in the presence of your uncle, that would offend propriety: and yet, yet you spurn me, cruel one?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Now, be calm, without pathos. My niece will, as soon as she finds her words, tell you – –

Stay outside a moment. I must take my chance first. Right! the young lady is locked up, and the old man is going into the picture-gallery. (calling out) Quickly, come in. Your master remained behind, did he not?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Away, I say! we know such rodomontades. Locked up – hunger – scruples – yielding – obedience! Punctum!
Alas, alas, poor princess! Cruel, barbarous, treacherous, Turkish uncle – but he does not hear me. He is clattering down into the back wing. – Quickly, come in! Your master is here as well?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Good heavens, yes; I verily believe she is lying there in chains.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What need have I to find my words? I have but one word to say, and that word is No!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Ha! you ungrateful girl!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Certainly not! Two hundred ducats are yours, and then you may have yourself joined in wedlock with your girl without a care.

div.head: Ninth Scene.
div.stage: The Chambermaid. The Lover. The Servant.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Alas! She is locked in.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Sir, I am moved, and when I am moved, I do whatever one asks of me. – Speak, rogue’s-eye! "When, how, where shall I strike him?"

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What? You will not have me? truly, really, reliably, in fact, most certainly will not have me? Good! Good, my fair young lady! then I will not have you either, truly not, really not, reliably not, in fact not, most certainly not!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Do not let yourself be angered! Consider, worthy Mr. von **, that here there can be no question of will at all. Only heed your father’s will, and mine.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Barbarous tormentor of girls!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Just listen! I was eavesdropping: The accursed squire is to come tomorrow, perhaps even today.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Surely not. Only let him speak. – Go on, speak!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: How shall we get rid of the oppressor?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Nothing of counsel and nothing of listening! My pronouncement is, as it were, a votum Dei; for Deus in me, you may hear that in all my speeches.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense! Your father's word holds, and mine in this matter. My niece is not to be consulted, and the contract already lies beneath my notary’s pen.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Who should be listening? It would be indiscreet indeed if anyone eavesdropped where I am. Let the rascal speak on.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I have been spying on the old man. And I heard that the bridegroom is perhaps to come even today, definitely tomorrow.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Not that I mean to undertake anything against the suitor. That has happened a hundred times over. Let him scratch who itches; we have a smooth skin, says someone in the tragedy, at a moment, too, when the tragedy looks like a farce, and is for that very reason a true tragedy.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What do you say?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What contract? What notary? I am notary enough myself; I have gone through the Pandects, I have studied the Criminal Code, the Sancta Carolina; to the devil with all notaries when I am present; besides, no contract is needed here.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed! The matter is settled between your father and me. Nothing in it can be undone, and, in short and good: You must marry my niece.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Pah! All the same! What are such village dullards usually called in comedies? Sebastian Lämmerzahn, or Thaddäus Bocklümmel, Theophilus Feldkümmel, or Hans von Birken, or Jeremias von Eschen, or plain Plumper.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: You?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Hahaha!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well? What next?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: To the point!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Look at me, and you have seen him.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What do you say? Must? Sir, who must? No one must! The word was invented by some despot, some tyrant, some zealot! and folly has echoed it and made a creed of it. Do you take me for a simpleton? What? You say I must marry your niece. No, I do not have to marry her; but now I will marry her.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Aha! So we submit, do we?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Is he still in his right mind? (aside)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: But why do I mean to marry her? In order to stay here in this house, here, with you, where I shall find a thousand occasions to vex and torment you – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: To arms! The enemy is here! Forward! Attack! The bridegroom, the detested one – he is already arrived!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But how will you make it possible?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Excellent! I shall steal the letter, if there is any way to do it.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Only quickly now. I must change my clothes.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, is the devil tormenting you?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: No, but I mean to torment you.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Go, leave us.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Never! Now I stay here and marry, and then I shall vex you to death. I am expeditious, you shall not have long to wait.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well then, steal it, but do not let yourself be caught, and bring your spoil to me in the great vine-arbour in the garden.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Let me draw your attention to something. By means of the letter which your young lady’s uncle received yesterday, we might perhaps be able to – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: So we are to go, then?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: There is something wrong in the upper storey with that man.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: And yet I am to marry him?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I would you had him, and were seated with him at the world’s end.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: If it pleases you –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: In a word, I perform an action by which I make it plainly known that, although I spoke words to you that were not befitting, I am nevertheless the servant and you the master, that is what one calls a sharp drawing of the characters.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Noble. Almost too noble for a servant. Only let it not turn out in the end that you have actually had an education. Go on ahead!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Privileges of a cunning servant, such as I am to represent just now. When the comedy is ended, the actors are all equal again.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You read. You have a precious library. Good! I shall glue all the pages of your books together, so that the books, as it were, have no contents at all, which is already the case with most of them.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What an idea!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Indeed, sir! It is not the first time today that I have come here to speak with you. Earlier you were not to be spoken with.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I, poor tormented man!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Do not hope for any compassion from the audience. The audience has never yet had pity on a self-willed uncle who is well taken to task in a comedy. Such a comedy I mean to play with you. I shall so embellish your picture-gallery that you will have to hang the paintings face to the wall. I shall paint a wig-bag on your Flora and a pair of Ypsilanti-trousers on your Apollo; your sea-battle I shall set ablaze with phosphorus, and the Plauen Valley I shall colour caca-dauphin –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What impudence: have I not long since told you my opinion without reserve? And yet you come here to me again?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
The Lover.
sp.p: "And why not? Are you not the guardian of your young niece? I am here for the second time to-day, and demand to speak with you, because earlier you were not to be seen." Und warum nicht? Sind Sie nicht der Vormund Ihrer Fräulein Nichte? Ich bin zum zweitenmale heute hier, und verlange Sie zu sprechen, weil Sie vorhin noch nicht sichtbar waren.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I have already heard of this fresh proof of your tyrannical cruelty.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I will have you thrown out of the house.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I will submit to that; but only on condition that I do not then marry the young lady. If that satisfies you, then have me thrown out.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That may be done as soon as you have married my niece.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense! She will not be set free until she lies in new chains and bonds, namely, in the arms of him who is to come –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Very concisely spoken!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I am so now, and I mean to be so, even if I were not so. Besides, the matter is settled; my niece is incarcerated until she – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Free must my beloved be, free she shall become, and you, sir, you are the one who will yourself open the door of her prison.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Indeed, sir, you are short of words.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Truly? You think so? Oh yes, I am satisfied with myself, and that my languishing niece may also be satisfied with me, I have shut her up, and shall not set her free until – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Heavens above, what is going on here? One can already hear outside the dreadful uproar that is within. Who is the gentleman?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Alas! I am going.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He is here?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Truly? Who? He?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Had I not to try to lull the old man asleep? Why, he saw our ally with me.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: The questioning belongs to me. Who are you? Some marten in the hen-house; a lover, most likely, come to pass himself off as me? Is it not so? (mimicking him) You are the young Mr. von **, whom his father sends hither to marry the gracious young lady there – Hoho! We know everything! You are unmasked, the true one is already here, and you must clear the field – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I wished to set the old man’s mind at ease; and I think it has succeeded.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: He need not come any more; he is already here.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Haha! There we have it. Now off with you, Your Worship.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Do not trouble yourself.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: With joy I behold you; with delight, though also with a little astonishment.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: But do come to your senses.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Never! By no means! Absolutely not! Most decidedly not!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Why so? Fresh mad notions!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Indeed, sir, I am a little astonished at your appearance, though delighted –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Yet I shall appear once more.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well then, sir, this welcome leads me to hope that I shall please you more and more.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: And to this madman you would sacrifice your ward? Sir, consider your conscience, your peace, your happiness in life! (softly) The Spanish sheep, two hundred in number, on my little estate: you always liked them; give me your niece, and the sheep are yours.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Two hundred sheep for a single little lamb – a good bargain.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well then, strike it –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Must not my name be mentioned in so important a document? Therefore I must ask you what my name is, that no confusion may arise, no fraud take place. So then, sir, what is my name?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Naturally! Quite after the manner of modern scribblers; you do not think of what is needful, you fasten upon what is useless; otherwise you would long since have asked my name.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, how can I – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Assuredly, for you are not even clear with yourself, let alone with me. Were you so, you would long since have inquired of me about myself, would have asked who I am, what my name is – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Truly?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: As true as I am an honest man!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: And you take me for such a simpleton as to suppose I would answer that?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Thunder and lightning! How should I know what your name is?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I would not have her become my wife through compulsion; compulsion is hateful to me. – Ha! is that she coming?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: But enough for your instruction this time. Call for your young niece and present me to her.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: With pleasure! Join your hands! And you, sir, you all-knowing man, reasoner and prattler – leave my house. And you two, my dears, you will soon be travelling as well, I suppose?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well then, so you do know it! And yet you asked? And still, if we consider it rightly, you had to ask after all.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Naturally. There are examples – disguised lovers who steal a bridegroom’s name – who lead father, uncle, or guardian by the nose; thus you ought to have inquired.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Your niece is not, I trust, disinclined to a marriage with me?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: All the thousand devils! Sir, why do you drive me to swearing? What am I actually to do? Ask, and then not ask? Not ask, and yet ask again?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Today yet. Rely on it.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: And on your promise. Adieu, we shall meet again. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: I have nothing further to say but No, and No I shall, I must, I will say, so long as I have a tongue.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Deluded creature!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That would be the very devil! even if your niece were ten times an angel. You mean to force us, then? Good, I give in –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What? Has the devil got into him? (aside)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You are a botanist. I know it, you have even a reputation as a botanist, Sir Linnaeus is said to have learnt much from you, perhaps even to have gone to school under you. – Good! Force me, and I shall have your herbarium boiled into my wedding soup.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: You are mistaken, sir, I do not choose you for my husband.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What is this? (softly to her) I warn you!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: So indeed? You persist in this hasty, ill-considered, unreflecting, unweighed, precipitate, to me dreadful, outrageous, maddening No? Good, my fair proud one. – Manus manibus laxat! or however the proverb may go – As you treat me, so I treat you – tit for tat – as one calls into the wood, so the echo answers – If you come at me so, I come at you so! Know then the consequence of your No. It is this: I will not have you either!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: But, my heavens, you must listen to your father, to me, to my counsel.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: But good heavens, this sudden change –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What is that black-coat doing here? Here, where there is no business for him?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Indeed there is business for him. He is to set the matter between you and my ward in proper order, as her father wills it, as I will it, as my niece is to will it, and as you must; yes, sir, must!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: No, sir, no! A thousand times no!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Foolish girl, you dare?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Well then, has my beloved at last arrived?

set.p: (The scene is a room with side doors.)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: A trick of my own invention.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Speak! Is he drawing near?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: How this rose bends, glowing, over the forget-me-not – so, my love, shall you ever guard in my heart the remembrance of my chosen one. – But where is he? Has no hindrance befallen him? He knows the hour! Why then does he not come? But hush! I hear footsteps – Well? Is it you at last?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: All sorrow is now forgotten!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: With you, I am happy!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I never cease to hope.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: The rascal played so admirably that on the stage he could never miss the sly-servant parts, nor, indeed, the intriguer’s roles in general.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: More of that later. Now it is time to receive your beloved.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What do you think?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: The danger that threatens our love –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Triumph of love! What but yesterday afternoon spoke and embraced and kissed now clasps each other today with the same tenderness, with the same glow of passion!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Later on; now embrace your friend.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What? You mean to go? Not yet! The comedy is not ended; be so good as to consider, what are we to do when the true bridegroom arrives?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Joy of reunion, how it gladdens me!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Feel my love in this kiss!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Without my guardian’s consent to our marriage, my fortune is lost – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Something, at least!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The time has come! The bridegroom is arriving. There shall be no further delay. My ward must finally submit. Shall I have given my word to my old friend for nothing? No, my honest Feldkümmel! We of the old stamp keep what we promise. Your lad is said to be of good stuff, passably handsome, and to have learnt his trade. So, done! – Hey! Miss Niece! (rings; to the Chambermaid who enters) Call your young lady! (the girl exits) – She will resist; but it avails her nothing, nothing at all! – Well then, Miss Niece?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Not too hastily. Caution can never harm. Love shall not make me blind. Without my dowry I do not follow you; therefore let us – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Then, with my bride, I am over the hills and far away.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Rather would we, in the dark of night and fog –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Shall the uncle surprise you? Left about, young sir! Come, my young lady!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: No questions! Listen to me! Attend! Bestir yourself! You must please, you shall please. Whom? The young Mr. von **. He comes today, at latest tomorrow, and the moment he comes, you are his bride.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – The bridegroom grants!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What shall we do, little mouse?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I think we do as clever folk do, that is, the lovers.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dearest uncle and guardian –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Who would make a comedy-fool of me, that I must say yes –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well? What now, my fine-dressed damsel?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Already given to him in love – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Excellent! We may well rejoice. Let the bridegroom give himself over to despair. But he will not. I hear he has seen Paris and London. There one learns all kinds of worldly wisdom. So he will laugh at my prank, even if he saw it on the stage, and on the stage it will surely appear, since the scarcity of one-act prologues and epilogues is unspeakably great.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: The happiness of my youth – –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – an unhappy one, as none ever was –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Girl, do not vex me. You know my gout grows worse, and that when anger takes hold of me –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Then, in your opinion, I should be –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Exactly. A comedy in one act. But how shall we christen it?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Oh well; Love’s Pain and Prize.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Or: A Wedding Without the Bridegroom.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Or: A Bridegroom Without a Bride.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Or: O. A. C. R. Our Applause Comes Readily.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: The Comedy with Two Weddings

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Or: He, She, and the Old Man.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: The Old Man, He and She.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Or: She, He and the Old Man.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Or: The Old Man, She and He.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Or: She, the Old Man and He.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: He, the Old Man and She. – The play must be prodigiously fine, for it can bear a hundred titles. Is it not so, ladies and gentlemen?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Miss, moderate yourself, or – –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Spare me! Grant me time! Only a few months, a few weeks at least –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense! At an engagement girls do not die nowadays; so soon as there is talk of a bridegroom of flesh and bone –

Ah, alas! my poor young lady! Truly, he is shutting her in! (She listens at the cabinet) Yes, yes, he is taking out the key. – What is to be done now? (calling out) Hey! Sweetheart! Come in! Is your master there as well?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – upon whom they use force –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Away with you, misguided girl, who thinks herself above my fatherly care!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Declaim as you please; I shall lock you up nevertheless. You may make a tragedy of the affair; I follow my plan and take it from a merry and yet serious side – Forward, miss! (He leads her out.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – Do not further imagine that you are upon the stage with me.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What? Shall I, like the innocent Scottish queen, be sacrificed to death for the sake of my love?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well then, little treasure?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Compose yourself! Stratagem must help us.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: A well-filled purse shall be proof to you of my resolve.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Stratagem? With that I can serve.

div.head: Ninth Scene.
div.stage: The Chambermaid. The Lover. The Servant.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Abominable comedy-uncle!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Never, though I must turn myself into gold. For my beloved’s freedom I sacrifice all –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: How shall we drive the unwelcome guest away?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well then, tell us your plan – –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well then, we choose another means –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Barbaric, panderous procurer of bridegrooms!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Here is my plan. To execute it, since my reward is already counted out, is a trifle.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well then, speak, arch-rogue! – No one is eavesdropping on us?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What? You?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Since the matter is made difficult for me, I must use twice my wits.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Truly?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Appalling!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: To represent him bodily, leave that to me.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Speak, what is your intent?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: As you please. Stretch out your fingers and seize quick and true. At the greenhouse in the garden I shall expect you.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: A happy thought! the letter must be stolen from the old man. I will try my skill on it.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: There, dearest little rogue of all rogues, take this first as proof of my gratitude. (He gives her money.)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: The pit – assuming I stood before such – sees in me, of course, the genius by whom the whole play is steered; yet for all that I must not cease to be your servant. Even if, ex. gr., I go before you as bell-wether, I must first perform some act which marks you as master and me as servant.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Then shall we withdraw?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: The honour belongs to me, assuredly, but I shall make no use of it.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Such an act would be –?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: At your service: yes!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: And though you begged till your hair turned grey: I stand by my No!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Beg as you please to your heart’s content; but I deny to my heart’s content.

div.head: Twelfth Scene.
div.stage: (Both hurry in through the central door.)

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: You do me wrong. I desire only the girl; not the girl’s fortune; so let yourself be persuaded.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Your niece will be set free; you will be forced to set her free.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I already heard how you once again tormented the poor child with your barbarity. Tyrant that you are!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Sir, you try to drive me mad! but you shall not succeed. I will see your niece freed, for you will be made to free her.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Of course. Whoever refuses to let youthful folly run wild is a tyrant, a barbarian, a Turk –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: It’s none of my concern. Said – done! You shall not have the girl.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: A cruelty that, alas! must have become a habit with you; for you are a tyrant!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Where? Where is he then?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well now, the one who’s been promised!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: A carriage has stopped before the Red Rooster Inn. The young gentleman who stepped out of it is already heading toward our house.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well, who else? It’s him himself, and it must be.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: There you hear it! There is nothing for you to do here.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Ha! That’s how one leads a nosey suitor by the nose. He’s here – did you hear?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Sir, I have seen the world. I have been in London, Buxtehude and Katzenelnbogen, in Paris, in Querfurt and on the Hunsrück, in Schweinfurt and Hirschberg, in Schaffhausen and on Vogelsand, in Mölln and on Felsenburg Island, in Eipeldau and the Vierlanden near Hamburg, in Prenzlau, Pest and Buda, in Oczakow and in the United States, in Transylvania and Zweibrücken, in Hinterpommern and the Land of Wurste in Darmstadt and in the Lüneburg Heath –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Don’t shout so, and consider where you are –

div.stage: The Uncle. The Chambermaid. The Servant.

(The Latter is dressed conspicuously like a fop. He speaks in the Berlin, Saxon, Pomeranian, or Mecklenburg peasant dialect; whichever is easiest, or rather most mouth-filling, for the famous actor who makes this role his constant study. He may also jumble all dialects together; so long as it has effect; for on effect alone rests the value of a comedy.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: A thousand times welcome!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Hoho! Things must proceed quite differently. Only when you know my aptitudes, my abilities, my talents, my merits, my excellences, my peculiarities, my views, insights, prospects, intentions, overviews, and considerations, along with all my histories and poems, my compositions, modulations, connections, oppositions, improvisations and approbations, my scores and coloraturas, my technique, polytechnic and mechanics, practice and tactics, aesthetics and poetics, logic and demagogy, ornithology, periphrasis and allegory, my rodomontades and jeremiads, my plastic arts and gymnastics –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Stop! Leave a word for other people!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But I shall step forth again from the background into which you push me.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Sir, I am the one who speaks here, no one else! For I am wealthy, since I have money, and besides that, I am well read. And what have I read? Schiller’s plays, and Seven Girls in Uniform, who, when they came to Pest, grew to thirteen, or otherwise multiplied to that number. I have read Goethe’s works and Kurländer’s almanac comedies; Newton’s treatise and Cramer’s novels; Voltaire’s Pucelle and Klopstock’s odes; Shakespeare’s Coriolanus and The Restless Matron of Pfyrt; Hufeland’s Macrobiotics and Schilling’s Woman as She Is; Dante’s Inferno and the poems of the improvisatore Wolff; the Minnesongs and The Berliners in Vienna; the doctrine of the Infinite and Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre; Krusenstern’s Voyage Round the World and the famous comedy Come Here!; the poems of the Magyars and Heß’s Topographical Description of the City of Hamburg; Tieck’s Puss in Boots and Aubry’s dog; Engelmann’s Lithography and the Berlin Schnellpost –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, don’t make my head spin!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Hoho! I’d be a fool to tell you now what my name is.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: But, in the devil’s name, how am I supposed to –?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well then, for heaven’s sake! What is your esteemed name?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I trust your niece will have no objection –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The fellow is making me dizzy! And why now me again and not you? and not you, but me?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I nearly forgot she’s locked up. (aloud) At once, at once, sir. (With a gesture, handing the chambermaid a key.) Here is the key to my room, bring the young lady through there by the quickest way.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Shall be done. (Exit.)

div.head: Fifteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Servant. The Niece. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Love each other, marry each other, and then get to know each other. You’re betrothed.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Yes, yes, sir, out of caution. And if I were not myself? If I were a disguised lover of the young lady? If I wished to ensnare your niece by such means?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Why would you think that?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Because of your guardianship I shall slap a lawsuit upon you, prosecute it myself, win said lawsuit, thereby gain compensation and fees and you shall pay.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: None of that! I won’t listen; I won’t take anyone’s advice.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Oh yes, you will! My niece, that silly creature, isn’t being asked. The notary is already on his way here with the contract.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Ha! so my fate is sealed. You don’t want me, Miss, fine! then I don’t want you either! and no power on earth shall ever make me budge from this firm, final, irrevocable, unshakable decision, not even by the thousand-millionth part of a silk-thread. There, that’s my most rectified oath!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Rectify your duty instead, and take some advice!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I’ll jump out of my skin! The man is mad!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: And to a madman you want to marry me off?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Yes, so that he may become sensible, or fully insane.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Away with all these absurdities! A notary, in our situation, is one of them.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: No, sir. The notary is absolutely essential. I know what I stipulated with your honoured father concerning the dowry of my ward; that shall the notary affirm, and you will have to marry my niece.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, are you possessed?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Not yet; but if you drive me crazy, I’ll call you out with pistols. You shoot – I’m bullet-proof; I shoot – you drop!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Done! You’ll keep your word?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: On my honor. Now just add your name to the contract.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I should really ask. Surely you are the lover, the favored one, of this lady. The fellow who always reappears at the end of a comedy to lead home his dearest sweetheart, after other people have helped him out of his troubles.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Leave me alone!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: No! I won’t! You want to marry me to this lady who doesn’t want me: so I’ll marry you to your pale yellow anger, until it carries you to the grave.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Is that serious?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Absolutely!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: This very hour.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Only after my word is kept.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Do you want to murder me?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I’ll give you no peace, day or night. Exactly because you can’t stand brass music, I’ll blow my horn under your window until the lark rises or the crows screech their way out of town. Only when the sun’s up, or when the morning fog grows thicker and thicker, shall you get even an hour of sleep.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Yes, the rascal has played his part splendidly, and satisfied all parties completely.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Exactly! What becomes of the characters after a comedy ends, no famous author ever worries about that! He’s finished his play, that’s what matters! Even tragedians often don’t care beyond that. And my little prank today is enough material for a comedy at best.

div.head: Final Scene.
div.stage: The Lover. The Niece. The Servant. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Am I bewitched? What is happening?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: And us as well, no?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: It is not likely to be otherwise.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Recognise in me the cause of this catastrophe.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I saw him coming.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: The harshness of my guardian –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Dear girl, will I ever be able to rejoice in having him as mine?

div.titlePart: The Old Man Outwitted, so Goes the World.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I signaled him. He’ll be in any moment.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Quick! Is he here?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What letter?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: You’d think they hadn’t seen each other for seven years, and yet they talked and embraced only yesterday.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Sweet sympathy of hearts, how you drive me out to my own sweetheart, who’s surely already lurking nearby!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Relieve your heart, put it into words.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: My uncle’s intentions –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Not so fast! I need my dowry if I’m to go with you. With a young rascal like you, it won’t take long before someone asks: What shall we eat, what shall we drink, what shall we wear? Then my six thousand thalers are good advisers; so let’s think this through carefully – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Yes, yes! She must. Old friend, with whom I’ve spent so many a happy hour, I won’t break my word to you. – He writes that the boy is decent and has learned something solid. Well, well! We’ll put him to the test, though that may hardly be necessary. My old friend Michael Balthasar Lämmerzahn doesn’t lie. It would be an outrage to put him to the test. (He rings. The chambermaid enters) My niece is to come.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: As you command. (Exit)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The case shall be quickly settled. – Ha! the little bride! Well, Miss Niece?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: We’re talking about my trial, and I give the verdict; you’ll marry, miss!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Not my concern.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What care I for his process? I proceeded against you, and you have lost. You shall wed according to my will, that is my sentence!

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: But my heart already belongs – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What process? Fear my proceedings if you don’t obey –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: That interests no one.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I do believe the little lady is threatening me.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Uncle, consider – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – a foolish child –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: Uncle, I can hardly believe you were ever my dear father’s own brother –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: – a twisted little head that needs straightening.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
