sp.p: Off with you, I’m locking you up. Into the dark you go, since you’re a foolish girl who could have oil for her lamp and yet refuses it. March! until you come to your senses. (He leads her out.)

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – destined to perish in misery –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Call him at once, so we can decide what to do. The old man has gone. (The servant exits) – Oh misery upon misery! Good thing we aren’t performing a comedy. we’d have to drop the curtain from sheer confusion.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – to waste away in grief –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Out of my way! You’ll stay locked up until you obey. Sing from the opera if you like: "Vous qui protégez les amours, venez, venez à mon secours!" If people outside want to hear it – fine; it won’t move me. Only obedience will set you free.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: – to drain the cup of suffering –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: For instance, I straighten this crooked waistcoat of yours, bow, and say: At your service.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What do you mean by that?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: At your service! Sir, the buckle on your hat is askew. – May I? (He adjusts it, returns the hat, and bows silently.)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Yes, unless you object.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: I'm not, at least not for you. Your visit is perfectly clear to me in its purpose; and that purpose is a young lady and a handsome purse of money.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What have you against me?

A gentleman’s desk and a young lady’s knitting bag, those are two things a clever maid must know inside and out. Here’s proof of my expertise: I have the letter! – – But where are my allies? Already gone? Then I must find them quickly so the farce can begin.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What, sir? Do I not please you?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Listen to my plea. I have enough means to support a wife. – I – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Indeed I will, and namely – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: A reply only a man like you could give.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Exactly! so be it; I want it so, and to put an end to all this useless back-and-forth, I locked up that obstinate little comedy-lover so that she – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: But suppose I tell you that even if I had not won my lawsuit, I would still possess a considerable fortune. What then?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What are you doing here?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: I’m leaving.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well? Where is the newly arrived bridegroom of my niece?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Ah, ah, my dear Adonis, how do you like it so far?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well then, sir; I am expecting a guest – my house and my rooms are becoming too cramped for me, so – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Surprised? Delighted? Just wait, you’ll soon be overwhelmed the moment you begin to grasp even a fraction of me: you’ll be possessed by a thousand demons of stiffness, swooning, faintness, dissolution, and melting away in the ocean of reverence that washes around the rocky cliffs of my colossal knowledge.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Good heavens! a rather steep sort of knowledge.

div.head: Fourteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Chambermaid. The Servant.
(The latter in a ridiculous outfit, marking him as a dandy of the newest fashion. As nothing ages faster than fashion, the author wisely gives no costume description.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Welcome, welcome!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Of course you know my name; you received yet another letter from my father not long ago.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: "Well yes, but – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well then, for heaven’s sake! What is your name?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: All the devils, sir! why did you insist that I ask in that manner?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I tolerate no contradiction. The world belongs to the young, a famous writer once said; I believe it was Lavater, or Schikaneder, or – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well yes! As though I could not be someone else, or rather, as though someone else could not be me, in order to slip in here and, as a disguised lover, carry off your niece right under your nose.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Absolutely not, absolutely not –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: It would be a pity if she didn’t consent at once. A man can be found any day; but not a man like me. I trust your young lady niece won’t stand in her own light.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What? I must? Very well then! But it will cost you dearly. You love gardening, I know it, the whole world knows it – fine! On my wedding day I’ll lay waste to your garden until it looks like the wig of a village schoolmaster after the ABC boys have torn it to shreds.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The unfortunate fellow has lost his mind.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: And yet I am to become his wife? Oh, miserable me!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Silence, you cause of all this misery!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: To the devil with contract and notary!

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Not to the devil; I am not the wretched devil incarnate! And the notary shall bring the contract here to me, and I will sign it, and my niece will sign it, and you will have to sign it.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Are you mad?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: No, sir; but you shall be. I’ll heat your head so thoroughly that not even a cold-water bath will help you.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: I want no advice. I won’t listen to anything. Philosophers – and I am a philosopher, you can tell that from my entire bearing – philosophers, I say, take no advice and listen to no one but themselves.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: But my niece must. Everything is settled between us; the notary is already preparing the contract –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Who are you? I could very well ask. But my sharp mind has guessed it already. You are this lady’s lover. – Hoho! You want to enjoy the triumph and watch how this demoiselle submits to her uncle, how she gives me her hand and leads me on like a fool, forcing me to make you my household friend. Missed your mark, sir! I will not marry this young lady. I would sooner, on the spot, take that other girl to wife, she seems to me still undecided enough.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Most assuredly! My niece is yours. – And you, you ridiculous traveller, philosopher, ornithologist, or whatever else you pretend to be – leave my house at once! (to the Lover.) You will be travelling soon as well, with your bride, I presume?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Heavens, at least let me explain – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: You hear it, I don’t want to hear anything, and I won’t stop tormenting you until you’re past hearing and seeing –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Oh yes, sir! I know your favorite hobbies, among others your shell and butterfly collection. Good! On my wedding day I’ll pound your shells into powder and serve them to you in Madeira wine; your butterflies I’ll release so the street boys can chase them.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Well then, within an hour we’ll settle the matter in writing. Take the girl – God bless you both! The stagecoach leaves today. For your information, Mr. Philosopher and rambling improviser. – When are bride and bridegroom travelling?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What right have you to ask? Why are you meddling with the most intimate family matters? This is my bride – and this is the bride’s uncle, my second father, so to speak, who has destined me for life’s greatest happiness, and to whom I shall return the favour by making his earthly life a hell, because he – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: For God’s sake, the man is raving! I know him – (secretly to the Uncle) He was locked up in Bückeburg two years ago already on account of – (points to forehead)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: What are you saying!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Oh, certainly! Let him go on. Rather hear me. I shall go even further, I shall take your niece without a dowry. Are you content now? Do you consent?

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: You’ll give me that in writing?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: This very day.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: And the two of us as well, I hope?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Yes, that was one of my little pranks.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: No matter, by then we’ll be far away.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: To Switzerland!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: To the land of freedom.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Wollen Sie mich rasend machen?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Ja, mein Herr, das will ich. Ich will in Ihrem Hause das Unterste zu oberst kehren. Ich will Sie ängstigen, quälen, verfolgen, todt ärgern –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Undoubtedly. Only the title is missing.

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: "A trifle! the play is called: Love’s Joy and Love’s Pain.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: Love’s Pain and Love’s Joy.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Or: He Who Has the Luck Wins the Bride.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: He Who Wins the Bride Has the Luck.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Not always! so I propose: The Letter from Zimpelshausen, or: The Bridegroom on the Road.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Or: The Bridegroom Without a Bride – but enough with the "ors". The honored audience may choose for itself. Anyone can make titles; it’s the play, especially the comedy, that usually causes trouble. Just look at the critical journals, articles: Fine Arts, etc. ibid.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Wonder no more, my love. Thanks to that rascal’s trick, all obstacles to our union have fallen away.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Sir, have I earned my reward? What if the real young Mr. von ** actually shows up?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Delightful! Then I’ve achieved the true goal of my scheme, namely this adorable little handful. Let the bridegroom, if he indeed should come, find his bird flown. – What is that to us? For us, the whole matter ends as a comedy?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Patience, he isn’t far now.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What lies closest to both our hearts.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Away! Out to my waiting Seladon, so I can share love’s manna with him as well. (Exit.)

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Nonsense! Your sweetheart, Mr. **, is not my man; he’s one-sided, and has few means, both in head and purse –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: What? You take me for – –

sp.speaker: The Niece.
sp.p: My Guardian, I am no wench, but a – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: No delays, no postponements, no time to think it over. I have no patience for such newly-poetic frippery. In my day, children and subordinates were taught to obey. Nowadays they think themselves super-clever and mock old age.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Off with you! You’ll be locked up. If your lover were nothing but a skeleton, I’d do it just like in the ballad, tie the two of you together and throw you into the dungeon.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.stage: (peeking through the central door, then entering.)

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Count on it, he’s waiting.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Why wouldn’t he? He’s standing outside as if nailed to the spot.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.stage: (looks through the door first, then enters.)

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Patience! Only stratagem can save us.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Just as I thought. And if you pull it off, you won’t go unrewarded.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Then he truly has her – –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: That’s exactly how a true lover would say it.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Tyrannical uncle!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: If you help, don’t worry about your reward.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: So she’s imprisoned?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Stratagem? – Pomade to me!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Well, then we can surely use some other means – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Detestable pander!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Heavens no, that would ruin our whole plan. – Come now, out with it, you rascal!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: What? Only let not my reputation suffer thereby; and nothing from some worn-out old comedy trick –

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: How do we go about chasing off that squire of a bridegroom?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: The old man will drive me insane with his contracted bridegroom.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: No matter. I divine his name already. Thaddäus Bocklümmel or Bastian Feldkümmel or Theophilus Lämmerzahn or Plumper plain and simple – yes, so must he be called. – "There must be lightning!" says Johanna von Montfaucon, who is known to employ only classical expressions.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Can it be?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Heavens!

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: What is the meaning of this?

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: I perceive!

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: Yes, who knows that!

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: The extraordinary has occurred; yet in the distress itself lies deliverance. – You, who truly know nothing, know this: that the contracted bridegroom is already here.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: 'Tis I! Am one of the lost souls, who shall go for wool and return home shorn. "Such is the lot of beauty on earth!" – What is his name again, the fair contracted one?

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Here, something on account of my gratitude. (He gives her money.)

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Here, here! Take this first as encouragement in your noble occupation.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: It is impossible to tell you that. I could have confided it to the chambermaid. I dare not confide it to you; that would be to make you of age in a matter wherein you must for the present remain a minor.

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: Well? What action though – –

sp.speaker: The Lover.
sp.p: You will be compelled to set your niece at liberty again.

sp.speaker: The Chamberm.
sp.p: What the deuce are you doing here?

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Calmly, sir; for only I have to speak here! Who am I? A rhetorician and historian, a Platonist and anatomist and mnemonist, a magister and polyhistor, a connoisseur and a patron, a critic and politician, a belletrist and a purist and an antagonist. – I have breakfasted on the Brocken and dined at Vesuvius, have eaten grapes in Saint Helena and stockfish at the Shetlands, have drunk porter in London and Chateau-neuf in Paris, have seen the ballet in Naples and in Pest the seven maidens in uniform, have made a journey through the panoramas of the Brothers Suhr and have travelled on the trekschuit from Amsterdam to Maastricht; therefore – –

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: Sir, I should like to show you the door at once.

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: How wise you pretend to be and how little you are so! Sir, I am not disinclined to take you for a moral philosopher who delivers a panegyric to the fashionable world. Yet you must know my name! Why do you pretend, then, as if you knew it not? Why do you deny your actual self, your peculiar nature, your true essence, your ideal or real self, your inner man?

div.head: Fifteenth Scene.
div.stage: The Uncle. The Servant. The Niece. The Chambermaid.

sp.speaker: The Uncle.
sp.p: The young Mr. von ** – My niece –

sp.speaker: The Servant.
sp.p: Well, I orientate, secure, palisade, entrench, provision myself gladly on all sides, toward all sides, against all sides – –
